The Past Ten Years: Psychoanalysis in the United States, 1980-1990

Edward Weinshel MD and Owen Renik MD

Owen Renik

2625 Scott Street
San Francisco, CA 94123

Owen Renik  

For psychoanalysis in the United States, the eighties have been a period of rapid movement and dramatic change, a time during which trends that arose in previous decades appear to have achieved visible consolidation. These shifts have encompassed theory, practice, and our organizational structure; and all have been influenced by cultural evolution and social pressure. Later in this essay we shall discuss a number of specific areas in which, we believe significant changes have taken place. We begin, however, with some general observations.

It is our impression that the last ten years have seen a movement, overall, away from categorical insistence on staunch psychoanalytic propositions and toward increasing self-inquiry: we analysts appear more comfortable in acknowledging the limits of what we do know and the tentative nature of many of our established formulations. This greater tolerance for uncertainty suggests, by implication, an underlying increase in genuine confidence regarding the reliable achievements of psychoanalytic understanding. Freud, Gisela, Silberstein, and the Repudiation of Femininity

Donald Silver MD

Donald Silver

26111 Fourteen Mile Road, #102
Franklin, MI 48025

Donald Silver  

The aim of this essay is to examine the teenage Freud through the letters he wrote as an adolescent. The letters suggest a possible explanation for his ideas about female psychology. I refer particularly to his “bedrock” statement of 1937 and his conviction that “The repudiation of femininity can be nothing else than a biological fact, a part of the great riddle of sex” (p. 252). The key word here, as I see it, is “repudiation.” I think the letters illustrate Freud's repudiation of an intense experience when he was 16 years old, his reaction to which was rooted in his own unresolved oedipal conflict. The source for this explanation is the recently published correspondence between Freud and his intimate friend Eduard Silberstein when they were both 16 years old, correspondence now available in English (Boehlich, 1990). The letters tell us that Freud had an experience so powerful that he had to repudiate its importance almost at once, that it took place in Freiberg, where Freud was born and lived for his first three years, that it had oedipal reverbations, that it had to be shared with Silberstein, and that it had to be denied. These letters, together with a few he wrote to another friend, Emil Fluss (see E. Freud, 1969) and other material, allow us to trace the experience as well as its aftermath.

Dr. Silver is an assistant Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, Wayne State University College of Medicine; he is also a Lecturer at the Michigan Psychoanalytic Institute.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Prologue

Melvin Bornstein MD

Melvin Bornstein

Melvin Bornstein  

In the first issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry the editors wrote, “We believe this to be a promising era of diversity and creative ferment in psychoanalysis….” The creative ferment they referred to evolved from an influx of ideas during the previous two decades that began to alter the theory and clinical practice of psychoanalysis from the models given to us by Freud and his analytic followers and subsequently elaborated by Hartmann in the United States, and Melanie Klein, Anna Freud, Winnicott, and others in England. Notwithstanding the elegance and intricacy of the analytic models available in the forties and fifties, many analysts found significant deficiencies that made it difficult to bridge abstract theory to clinical practice.

The descriptions of clinical practice frequently presented in scientific forums and teaching situations were different from actual occurrences in the clinical setting because of the impossibility of describing clinical experience with the concepts and models that were available in the early sixties. Thus, the difference between description and performance became fertile ground for dissatisfaction, defensiveness, and idealization among psychoanalysts.

The psychoanalytic landscape began to alter during the sixties and seventies. Arlow and Brenner (1964) and Brenner (1979) elaborated the structural theory and emphasized the place of unconscious fantasy and depressive affects within the conceptualization of the working of the mind.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Epilogue

Melvin Bornstein MD

Melvin Bornstein

Melvin Bornstein  

Some of the problems facing psychoanalysis in the nineties as well as some of the trends visible in the eighties can be discerned in the preceding pages. What is perhaps most notable, however, is the diversity of mood among our contributors. Weinshel and Renik view the decade with obvious approbation and especially appreciate the trend to a less doctrinaire approach. Their point finds immediate illustration in Meissner's willingness to employ more than a single model to explain clinical phenomena. Pulver makes a similar point in recognizing the increasing flexibility with which psychoanalysts apply their theory to clinical encounters. This general approval of what the eighties have wrought is bolstered by Etchegoyen's optimistic report from the southern hemisphere. And from across the ocean, Meares also sounds pleased with recent developments. Cooper, on the other hand, though he views theoretical pluralism with approval, anticipates difficulties in our maintaining our psychoanalytic identity as nonmedical psychoanalysis becomes the order of the day.

Three of our contributors, Wolf, Mitchell, and Stolorow have used the occasion to set forth their own ideas. Wolf rejects the idea of the analyst as an Olympian and urges, as a means of moving toward a more egalitarian view of the analytic situation, that we think in terms of analyst and analysand rather than of analyst and patient. Gedo, on the other hand, deplores what he sees as a descent by the analyst, if not from Olympus, at least from a humanistic height to a depth of crass materialism and mere technology.

responseSet.abstract:

Epilogue

George Moraitis Issue Editor

George Moraitis

George Moraitis  

The in-depth exploration of any psychological phenomenon, no matter how well circumscribed clinically, will inevitably necessitate the broadening of the boundaries of the exploration in order to place it in context. Phobias are no exception.

For a long time the clinical and theoretical study of the phobic symptom was dominated by the imaginative interpretation of the patient's unconscious fantasies and their vicissitudes. It is hard to overestimate the enormous appeal of such interpretations for the analyst. It can be compared to the reaction Freud reported when he visited the Acropolis, “So all this really does exist, just as we learned in school.”

With time, however, the analyst's excitement has been tempered by the fact that many of the phobic patients neither share the analyst's excitement about the interpretations of the unconscious fantasies nor improve clinically as a result of such interventions.

The preceding contributions illustrate that the contemporary psychoanalyst has taken notice of the fact that all phobias cannot be effectively dealt with simply by the interpretation of their symbolic meaning. Instead, our contributors, to various extents, approach phobias as a manifestation of a more general and basic pathology, structurally and developmentally.

This development has important clinical implications because the phobic symptom is no longer the main focus of the analyst's attention, but a stepping stone in addressing the deeper level of psychopathology upon which the whole personality organization rests.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Epilogue

Philip Escoll Issue Editor

Philip Escoll

Philip Escoll  

It is evident from the preceding papers that, as in most psychoanalytic matters, we are indebted to Freud for opening the door to our understanding of female psychology and development. It is also evident from these papers that we have progressed well beyond Freud in our understanding of the female psyche, and we must continue to do so. Freud was limited by the phallocentric view of his times, which he adopted. He failed, as Elizabeth Young-Bruehl points out, to revise his theories of female development in the light of his later theoretical conceptualizations in other important areas. As the present time lag in utilizing new insights into the female psyche demonstrates, it is not easy to depart from previously established ideas and theories.

In addition to problems posed by his own personal conflicts, experiences, and biases, Freud did not have the advantage of being influenced by modern culture with its changes in the role of women, or of the systematic studies utilizing infant and child research observations, the accumulated data from adult analysis over many years, and information derived from child analysis. Freud recognized the importance of preoedial influences on the female and her relationship with mother, for example, but he did not utilize these ideas in his theories.

The new findings represented in the modern literature, as well as in the papers in this issue, have important theoretical implications. As such, they also are significant for the psychoanalytic treatment of women.

Psychoanalysis: The Past Decade

Arnold Cooper MD

Arnold Cooper

525 East 68th Street, P-155
New York, N.Y. 10021

Arnold Cooper  

Two phenomena, the increased acceptance of psychoanalytic theoretical pluralism and the modification of our psychoanalytic professional structures around the settlement of the famous “lawsuit,” signaled the major changes of the decade of the eighties. It is conceivable that the end of the eighties, in psychoanalysis as in the “real world,” may mark the end of several of our own cold wars. Our previously relatively orderly theoretical borders, once forming an iron curtain that was impervious to ideas from “the other side,” now seem permeable and even welcoming. The tenacious maintenance of certain theoretical and political boundaries — our Berlin walls, if you wish — that seemed so important until recently, and that has been the source of friction and battle for decades, has seemed increasingly quixotic rather than scientific; perhaps this will lead to an era of greater psychoanalytic cooperation and discourse, if not harmony. As in the “real world,” this peace may be accompanied by enormous confusion and a period of disorderly growth and perhaps regression, as we attempt to adapt to new circumstances.

Dr. Cooper is Professor of Psychiatry, New York Hospital-Cornell University Medical Center; Supervising and Training Analyst, Columbia University Center for Psychoanalytic Training and Research.

Psychoanalytic Education and Research: A Transformative Proposal

Robert Wallerstein MD

Robert Wallerstein

401 Parnassus Avenue
San Francisco, CA 94143

Robert Wallerstein  

The invitation to write a paper on any topic of my choice that relates to developments in psychoanalysis over the last ten years is unusually generous, but it enjoins some care in distinguishing what is significant and of abiding interest or concern from the more transient or peripheral. Recently, together with Edward Weinshel, I wrote a comparable paper by invitation for the Psychoanalytic Quarterly, on The Future of Psychoanalysis (Wallerstein & Weinshel, 1989). There we developed our approach to that large canvas along six dimensions: the nature of psychoanalysis as a science, its nature as a discipline, psychoanalytic education and its relationship to the wider university world, the nature of psychoanalytic research, the nature and scope of professional practice, and the institutional expression of psychoanalysis in the International Psychoanalytic Association and its component organizations.

Here I want to focus on and develop further two of these—the nature and state of health of psychoanalytic education and of psychoanalytic research, both beset, I believe, by persistent and intractable problems and usually considered separately from one another, though they are clearly intricately interdependent.

Dr. Wallerstein is Professor of Psychiatry, University of California, San Francisco, School of Medicine; Training and Supervising Analyst, San Francisco Psychoanalytic Institute.

Phobias and the Pursuit of Novelty

George Moraitis MD

George Moraitis

180 North Michigan Avenue
Chicago, IL 60601

George Moraitis  

Freud's formulations on phobias underwent a continual change that reflects the evolution of psychoanalysis, theoretically and clinically. Despite these changes, however, Freud always maintained, in one form or another, the distinction between phobias as a psychoneurotic symptom and phobias as a symptom of “actual neurosis” the latter carrying the inclusion of a biologically based condition.

For a long time in the clinical situation, the analysis of phobias has been dominated by Freud's (1909) case of Little Hans, in which he conceptualized phobias within the category of a hysterical neurosis. Phobics were identified as the hysterics who are unable to repress their unacceptable wishes and fears and instead displace them onto other objects and situations. The phobic symptom, like the dream, was described as another royal road to the unconscious, the analysis of which one hoped would lead to the uncovering of the unconscious wish and fear of retribution.

In the actual clinical situation, this proved to be a very hard road to travel. Attempts to utilize the psychoanalytic conceptual model in the treatment of phobias have often been ineffective. Freud (1919, pp. 165-166) identified this difficulty when he wrote: “One can hardly master a phobia if one waits till the patient lets the analysis influence him to give it up.

Dr. Moraitis is Training and Supervising Analyst, Chicago Institute for Psychoanalysis; he is on the faculty at Northwestern University.

A Decade of Psychoanalytic Praxis

W. Meissner S.J.

W. Meissner

129 Mount Auburn Street
Cambridge, MA 02138

W. Meissner  

As this journal comes to celebrate its tenth year of its existence, it can look back at a decade of rather remarkable ferment in psychoanalysis. The ferment can be most easily recognized, first in the changes that have evolved in the organizational and institutional aspects of the field, and second in the swirl of theoretical currents that are presently awash in the psychoanalytic tub. My impression is that there has also been significant ferment in the development of psychoanalytic technique or praxis. In the present essay, I would like to try to identify and assess some of these possible directions in praxis.

The institutional gyrations are matters of public record and thus identified. The theoretical turmoil is a bit more complex, but nonetheless flourishes quite noisily on the pages of many journals and assaults the ears in many professional meetings. But the shifts in how analysis is practiced are more subtle and hidden—veiled behind the closed doors of individual consulting rooms and more masked than unveiled in the more public contexts of collegial exchange. Matters of technique and the understanding of aspects of the psychoanalytic process are written about, but one is never sure of the extent to which what is written about in the public forum corresponds to what transpires in the many contexts of ongoing interaction between analyst and patient.

Dr. Meissner is Training and Supervising Analyst, Boston Psychoanalytic Institute; University Professor of Psychoanalysis, Boston College.

A View From the Other Side

Russell Meares Acad. D.P.M. (London) F.R.A.N.Z.C.P., F.R.C.Psych.

Russell Meares

Westmead NSW 2145
Australia

Russell Meares  

This issue celebrates ten years of Psychoanalytic Inquiry, a journal that has played its own particular and valuable part in the recent evolution of psychodynamic thinking. The “panel” format, which has allowed the expression of diverse, and at times contradictory views, is not only unusual but also potentially creative, fostering dialogue out of which new ideas can emerge. The open-mindedness implicit in this approach, so it seems to me, necessarily arises from the empathic stance of self psychology to which developing theory Psychoanalytic Inquiry has contributed. My title, however, refers not only to this viewpoint but also to my invited task, which is to address the changes in psychotherapy in Australia over the last decade. The selection of theme is inevitably personal and focuses on a psychology of self.

Ideas can only grow in a cultural milieu. The character of a particular culture will influence the way in which those ideas will manifest themselves. The Freudian thesis, for example, had different forms in nineteenth-century Vienna, in Chicago in the nineteen-thirties, and in Paris in the sixties. The ideas upon which a psychotherapy is based must be related not only to an intellectual tradition but also to the culture in which it acts. In this way it will have a vitality which encourages originality and creativity.

Dr. Meares is Professor of Psychiatry, University of Sydney; Director of Psychiatry, Westmead Hospital, Sydney, New South Wales.

George Moraitis  

Phobias and panic states have in recent years become the subject of intense interest in psychiatry. Psychiatric journals are flooded with publications on the biological and behavioral aspects of these conditions which have to some extent obstructed the reader's awareness of the contributions of psychoanalysis to the understanding and treatment of these conditions. It would be ironic if, during this period of the widening scope of the clinical applications of psychoanalytic treatment, the psychoanalyst were to relinquish to the nonanalytically oriented therapist this crucial clinical field upon which psychoanalytic theory and its clinical applications are based.

By devoting this issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry to the recent advances in the psychoanalytic understanding and treatment of phobias, we aim to provide our readers with a more balanced view of our present knowledge about phobias, and alert them to the fact that the contemporary psychoanalyst shares with Freud his intense interest in the subject and continues the search for a more effective conceptualization and treatment of these conditions, which takes into account new data and observations from within and without the field of psychoanalysis.

The classical approach in analyzing phobias aims to uncover the unconscious fantasy operating behind the symptom and reconstruct the original trauma, facilitating in the process the patient's capacity to come to terms with it.

The Evolution of Freud's Conceptualization of Phobias

David Spira MD

David Spira

180 N. Michigan Avenue
Chicago, IL 60601

David Spira  

The purpose of this article is to review the evolution of Freud's understanding of phobias, with a particular eye toward the distinction he made between actual neuroses and psychoneuroses. This focus is relevant to the question of biologic versus psychologic factors in producing pathology. Because the subject of phobias occupies a central position in psychoanalytic theory by virtue of its intimate relation to an understanding of anxiety and defense, the reciprocity between Freud's evolving models of mind and his ideas on phobia will also receive attention.

This review is organized in accordance with the three major phases of Freud's theorizing. During the early phase, which lasted until 1905, he thought phobias were caused by traumatic events and their associated affects. Phase two, from 1905 to 1923, was characterized by his rejection of the seduction hypothesis and the development of the libido theory. Working within the context of the latter, Freud described two forms of phobia, one emphasizing a psychogenic mechanism, the other, designated as actual neurosis, explained by an accumulation of libido — a cumulative biologic factor.

Dr. Spira is on the faculty of the Institute for Psychoanalysis of Chicago.

Aman in his late 30s, in the eighth year of an analysis undertaken because of paralyzing difficulties in love and work that had driven him to despair, managed at long last to fall in love for the first time. Contrary to his invariable habit in relation to the countless women he had discarded in a career of Don Juanism, he was not preoccupied with listing the alleged shortcomings of his inamorata's status or prestige. In fact, he was almost craven in his tolerance of her initial lack of commitment to their relationship, and he refrained entirely from raising objections to her behavior and preferences, although he often found these rather difficult to bear. Only certain dreams of vengeance on a woman (in the manifest content, this was sometimes explicitly his mother) — especially revenge by means of sexual infidelities — betrayed the fact that he was enraged by these deprivations and once again on the verge of lapsing into the guerrilla warfare that had characterized his dealings with his parents for over three decades.

In these circumstances, I predicted a rupture of this important relationship — the first contingency to have relieved the patient's chronic depressive mood — unless he could make his needs clear to his beloved and gain her cooperation in mitigating his dissatisfactions.

Psychoanalytic inquiry is celebrating the successful completion of its first decade as a vital forum of unfettered discourse; at the same time, we are on the threshold of being able to commemorate the centenary of our origins as a discipline, Sigmund Freud's initial psychotherapeutic efforts as a private practitioner. Psychoanalysis of the eighties presents itself for our consideration as a complex, changing, and very much alive discipline which may be contemplated from different angles, thus making it seem difficult to achieve a view of it as a whole. Waiving the possibility of carrying out such a synthesis, this paper will concern itself with the relationship between clinical endeavors and psychoanalytic theories, in the hope that this road will lead us to problems that genuinely interest the psychoanalyst of our times.

In presenting my points of view, which are necessarily limited and fragmentary, I should like to start by saying that our times are heavily influenced by the 50th anniversary of Freud's death. I feel we have only recently begun to be aware of his absence and the loss this entails, to recognize that he is no longer with us.

If we take a bird's-eye view of how the psychoanalytic science has evolved, we are faced with a clear-cut dividing line that coincides with the end of Freud's life.

Psychoanalysis is in the midst of a crucial transitional phase. We are struggling with the problem of how to assimilate and utilize our past traditions to best serve our current needs. Many of the most important contributions to psychoanalytic theory and clinical practice in the past ten years have been concerned, either explicitly or implicitly, with this broad and complex project of assimilation—the sorting out of what is still useful and the discarding of what no longer applies. In previous papers introducting another perspective on the psychoanalytic theory of aggression (Buie et al., 1983; Meissner et al., 1987), our study group on aggression presented what we felt was a more authentically psychoanalytic and more purely motivational understanding of aggression that suited the findings on and the vicissitudes of it as manifested in the psychoanalytic process.

The essential elements of that understanding can be summarized as follows:

Aggression is not simply a biologically based drive in a constant state of activity or discharge, but a biologically rooted drive capacity that requires appropriate stimulus conditions to elicit activation or response.

This view of aggression clearly diverges from the classical drive notion. The difference is clear in the developmental context: drive theory would see the development of aggression as a process in which the mental apparatus strives to integrate the aggressive drive derivatives impinging on it from below, i.e., from an innate biologically given drive; our motivational theory would see the development in aggression as reflecting the organism's experience of dealing with and overcoming obstacles in the course of which drive potentialities or capacities are activated and integrated.

The Mental Representation of the Clitoris: The Fear of Female Sexuality

Nancy Kulish PHD

Nancy Kulish

29260 Franklin Road, #104
Southfield, MI 48034

Nancy Kulish  

While early psychoanalytic theory made the clitoris the predominant focus of theories of female sexuality, current writers have raised challenges about its role and function in female sexuality and sexual development. Yet it is striking how little has been said about the mental representations of the clitoris, insofar as the mental life is the realm with which psychoanalysis deals. It is my purpose in this paper to search for possible representations of the clitoris in dreams, fairy tales, and clinical data from the psychoanalytic situation to see what light, if any, such an exploration may throw on the current questions regarding female sexuality. I also attempt to explore why representations of the clitoris have gone unattended in psychoanalytic writing and in mental life in general.

The Role of the Clitoris in Psychoanalytic Theories of Female Development

Freud's (1905, 1931, 1933) theories about the role of the clitoris in female sexuality can be summarized as follows: Before the discovery of the differences between the sexes, the little girl's sexual development is identical to that of the little boy's.

Dr. Kulish is Director of Psychology, Detroit Psychiatric Institute.

Sexual Identity, Trauma, and Creativity

Joyce McDougall D.Ed.

Joyce McDougall

60 Rue Quinacampoix
75004 Paris
France

Joyce McDougall  

This paper deals with two related themes. The first concerns the nature of trauma and the clinical and theoretical problems involved when a traumatic event arises concomitantly with psychoanalytic treatment. In general it may be stated that a catastrophic present-day event will prove to be traumatic (that is, subsequently giving rise to psychic reorganization of a symptomatic kind) only to the extent to which it reactivates earlier psychic trauma. A more specific theme concerns the relation of trauma to creative activity. In an earlier work (Meyers, 1988) I had proposed that creative work in any field requires the integration of the universal bisexual wishes of childhood and that failure to identify with the potential fertility of both parents due to impediments in this integration is a frequent cause of serious intellectual and creative inhibition. I shall here explore the unconscious significance of bodily trauma arising in the analytic situation and its subsequent regressive effects on creative activity.

To illustrate these themes, I have chosen a vignette of three consecutive sessions from the analysis1 of a woman who initially sought analytic help because of a severe writing block as well as a conflictual relationship with her lesbian lover, Frederika.

Joyce McDougall is a Member of the Paris Psychoanalytic Society; she is an Honorary Member of the Association for Psychoanalytic Medicine (New York).

Fear, Phobia, and Panic

Joseph Lichtenberg MD

Joseph Lichtenberg

1616 Eighteenth Street, N.W.,
Washington, D.C. 20009

Joseph Lichtenberg  

Anyone familiar with the extensive literature on fear (anxiety), phobias, and panic disorders is inevitably impressed by the complexity of the topic. One set of questions can be formed from within the traditional structural hypothesis (Spira). Is anxiety to be singled out as a special response pattern, which, as a signal, is central to the function of the psychic apparatus? Are phobias one of a group of psychoneuroses susceptible to straight-forward analysis of the conflicts, compromise formations, and symbolic meanings by classical psychoanalytic techniques? Are panic disorders the result of the failure of the ego to restrict anxiety to its signal function or to the failure to create a stable symptom (compromise formation) such as a phobia through symbolic representations and defensive activity? Another set of questions can derive from alternative perspectives cited or implied by one or more of our contributors. Is fear one of a group of basic affects, each having great psychological significance but none having special intrapsychic adaptational importance? An affirmative answer to this proposal brings into question the psychoanalytic tradition of distinguishing between fear and anxiety and assigning signal anxiety a central functional role. How are we to regard empirical data that indicates unusual difficulty in the analysis of many phobic patients? Are we failing to ascribe sufficient significance to residues of traumatization (Rocah)?

Dr. Lichtenberg is Editor-in-Chief of Psychoanalytic Inquiry and a member of the Faculty of the Washington Psychoanalytic Institute.

Rereading Freud on Female Development

Elisabeth Young-Bruehl

Elisabeth Young-Bruehl

82 Goose Hill Road
Chester, CT 06412

Elisabeth Young-Bruehl  

As sigmund Freud developed his view of female psychology, he indicated areas where he thought his conclusions were quite trustworthy and others where is insights were either untested or still tentative. A pattern has emerged in the criticism as Freud's view that has developed over six decades: where he felt most secure, criticism has been most vehement, sustained, and consensual; where he felt hypothetical or tentative, there has been lack of consensus and conceptual tangle.

This battle of sexuality theories is much too long and full of fronts for review in one article. What I would like to do is pursue a particular angle, inviting you to follow an exercise in what-might-have-been. Specifically, I will offer a review of the questions that Freud's theoretical revisions after 1920 might have raised had he reconsidered his views on female psychology in light of those revisions. This is only an exercise in historical-biographical reconstruction and theory-construction — I am not writing as a clinician on the basis of clinical experience, but as a historian. I do think, however, that this approach can illuminate current psychoanalytic thinking about female psychology.

1

The area of Freud's views on female psychology that he assessed as most secure was articulated clearly in his 1905 Three Essays.1

Elisabeth Young-Bruehl is Professor in the College of Letters at Wesleyan University and is a member of the Gardiner Seminar in Psychiatry and the Humanities at Yale University.

Pubescence: A Psychoanalytic Study of One Girl's Experience of Puberty

Ruth Fischer MD

Ruth Fischer

658 Black Rock Road
Bryn Mawr, PA 19010

Ruth Fischer  

Puberty is the coming of age, a time of sexual maturity, a coming to terms with one's body, a time of disengagement from parents and establishing relationships with peers. Burgeoning sexual maturity makes it necessary for the girl to confront her new body. Oedipal conflicts are revived, leading to regression and a reworking of infantile conflicts and relationships (Blos, 1979).

We have traditionally understood this as a time when the girl experiences a revival of awareness of her castrated state, which leaves her feeling inferior, humiliated, deprived, and envious, a time of renouncing her masculine strivings and accepting her femininity, renouncing her wish for a penis and substituting it with a wish for a baby. She is left infantile and dependent with a faulty superego, never totally abandoning her wish for her father (Freud, 1931; Deutsch, 1944). This is indeed a time of reworking of old feelings, feelings related to sexual difference and sexual maturity. It is not, however, a time of giving up masculinity and becoming feminine. The girl is already and always has been feminine.

Dr. Fischer is Training Supervising Psychoanalyst, Philadelphia Psychoanalytic Institute; she is a member of the Faculty, University of Pennsylvania School of Medicine and Senior Attending Psychiatrist, Institute of Pennsylvania Hospital, Philadelphia.

[[RunningHead]]

Prologue

Philip Escoll Issue Editor

Philip Escoll

Philip Escoll  

The view of females as inferior to males and the tendency of scientists to judge females by male standards has a long history. In her book Sexual Science Russett (1989) points out that Victorian anthropologists, biologists, and psychologists were so convinced that women were inferior that they inevitably were able to find “evidence” to support this conclusion, even if this required rationalization. Women were seen as playing an inferior part compared to men even in conception, the ovum being described as passive, the sperm filled with energy. Famous men of the age, such as Darwin, found it difficult to maintain their usual scientific objectivity in writing about women.

It was only natural that Freud, a product of the Victorian age, was influenced by the attitudes of that period. He too conceptualized women using males as the standard of comparison and therefore viewed women as deficient, for example, in superego development. Women puzzled him, witness his famous remark, “Was will das Weib?” (What does a woman want?”; Jones, 1955, p. 421). Freud was challenged in his views of female development by Jones, and also by Karen Horney and Clara Thompson. Women psychoanalysts have continued to be the most important influences in reshaping Freud's theories about female psychology, although others such as Helene Deutsch and J. Lampl-deGroot, were closely identified with Freud's ideas. Greenacre, Jacobson, and Kestenberg have made significant theoretical and clinical advances in this area.

Psychoanalytic Technique: Progress During the Past Decade

Sydney Pulver MD

Sydney Pulver

111 North 49th Street
Philadelphia, PA 19139

Sydney Pulver  

Changes in psychoanalytic technique, like changes in patients, take place slowly. They tend to be changes of emphasis rather than of substance, and they are almost always the outcome of debates that reach back many years. The changes in technique that have taken place over the past decade are no exception. They are the outgrowth of the debate about the scientific versus humanist view of psychoanalysis, a dialectic that can be found in Freud's earliest writings. The view of the psychoanalytic process as taking place in a relationship between two people with the analyst as participant-observer has slowly but surely gained ascendance over the earlier picture of the analyst as the objective observer using the dissecting table of the analytic couch. In this article, I will describe some of the ways these changes have been manifested. In doing so, I will be describing changes in what I think of as the “average expectable” technique practiced by eclectic adult analysts in the United States. My description will necessarily be subjective and value-laden, since I look favorably upon the direction in which psychoanalysis is going, and see these changes as advances.

Dr. Pulver is a Member and Training and Supervising Analyst, Philadelphia Psychoanalytic Institute; Clinical Professor, Department of Psychiatry, School of Medicine, University of Pennsylvania; Senior Attending Staff, Institute of Pennsylvania Hospital.

Robert Stolorow PHD

Robert Stolorow

11726 San Vicente Boulevard

Robert Stolorow  

Analysis … must turn from the study of Freud to the study of man. — Kohut

To my mind, the most important development in psychoanalysis over the past decade has been the growing recognition that intrapsychic phenomena must be understood in the context of the larger interactional systems in which they take form. Evidence of this trend can be found in the increasingly frequent appearance in the psychoanalytic literature of such terms as self-selfobject relationship (Kohut, 1984), two-person psychology (Modell, 1984), relational matrix (Mitchell, 1988), mutual influence structures (Beebe & Lachmann, 1988a, 1988b), and intersubjective context (Atwood & Stolorow, 1984; Stolorow et al., 1987).

Dr. Stolorow is a member of the faculty of the Southern California Psychoanalytic Institute and a member of the Core Faculty of the Institute for the Psychoanalytic Study of Subjectivity.

Ernest Wolf  

“I may begin by saying that psycho-analysis is not a child of speculation, but the outcome of experience; and for that reason, like every new product of science, is unfinished. It is open to anyone to convince himself by his own investigations of the correctness of the theses embodied in it, and to help in the further development of the study” (Freud, 1911, p. 207). Freud himself, throughout his life time, continued to study and correct his earlier findings and bequeathed us a science that he knew, like all other sciences, to be unfinished. Not all of Freud's students have always taken the above comments of the master as seriously as they deserved. In retrospect it seems that the flood of psychoanalytic advances slowed to a trickle after Freud's death. To be sure, the work of the ego psychologists and of the object relations theorists continued important lines of investigation that had been started in Freud's time. But one looks in vain for fundamental breakthroughs on the order of, for example, Freud's abandonment of the seduction theory or of his replacement of the topographical with the tripartite model of the psychic apparatus.
